q1: SELECT b.name AS bar, COUNT(DISTINCT f.drinker) AS num_drinker, AVG(s.price) AS avg_price, (SELECT f1.drinker FROM frequents AS f1 WHERE f1.bar = b.name ORDER BY f1.times_a_week DESC, f1.drinker ASC LIMIT 1) AS most_reg_drinker FROM bar AS b LEFT JOIN frequents AS f ON b.name = f.bar LEFT JOIN serves AS s ON b.name = s.bar GROUP BY b.name ORDER BY num_drinker DESC, b.name ASC
q2: SELECT td.total_count, td.bar, avg_p.avg_price, mfd.drinker FROM (SELECT frequents.bar, COUNT(frequents.drinker) AS total_count FROM frequents GROUP BY bar ORDER BY bar DESC) AS td, (SELECT serves.bar, AVG(serves.price) AS avg_price FROM serves GROUP BY bar ORDER BY bar ASC) AS avg_p, (SELECT mfds.bar, MIN(mfds.drinker) AS drinker FROM (SELECT ft.bar, ft.drinker, ft.times_a_week FROM frequents AS ft JOIN (SELECT ff.bar, MAX(ff.times_a_week) AS times_max FROM frequents AS ff GROUP BY bar) AS bar_max ON bar_max.bar = ft.bar AND ft.times_a_week = bar_max.times_max ORDER BY ft.bar ASC, ft.times_a_week DESC, ft.drinker ASC) AS mfds GROUP BY mfds.bar) AS mfd WHERE td.bar = avg_p.bar AND td.bar = mfd.bar AND avg_p.bar = mfd.bar ORDER BY td.total_count DESC, td.bar ASC, mfd.drinker ASC

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent due to the different methods they use to determine the 'most regular drinker' and the overall structure of the queries.
counterexample_dsp: The difference arises in how the 'most regular drinker' is determined. Q1 orders by 'times_a_week' in descending order and 'drinker' in ascending order, while Q2 orders by 'times_a_week' in descending order and 'bar' in ascending order. This can lead to different results if there are ties in 'times_a_week' or if the 'bar' order affects the final selection.
